solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Smith possibly loads millions into vessel (9)

indicators.note: rafts, as in 'rafts of' = loads, is the inner piece
RAFTS and M go into the vessel

blocks.note: a can is a vessel; it opens round the rest
rafts of something = loads of it

explanation.surface: A cargo of cash being stowed in a ship's hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' tempts you towards a boat, and CRAFT does appear in the answer, but only as a coincidence of the assembly. 'Loads' looks like a verb and is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A smith is a skilled worker with metal, a kind of craftsman; 'possibly' flags the example.

clue.text: Better feature after you texted brother (8)

indicators.note: CHIN comes after CAP and U

explanation.surface: Someone improving their looks after messaging a sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' reads as an adjective and is the verb 'cap'. The brother is not a sibling but a friar of the Capuchin order.
explanation.definitionFit: A Capuchin is a friar of a Franciscan order, and friars are addressed as Brother.

clue.text: A stump up when root cut in tree (5)

indicators.note: in a down entry the root is the bottom, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: SPEND (stump up = pay) loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A tree-surgeon's bill for felling and taking out a stump.
explanation.walkthrough: To stump up is British slang for paying up, so SPEND. 'Root' suits a tree, but here it is the foot of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is a poplar tree known for its trembling leaves.

clue.text: Underground fluid protects masking tape, ultimately (3-6)

indicators.note: a fluid thing takes a new shape, so the letters rearrange
the rearranged letters cover the E
ultimately = in the end, so the word's final letter is the one used

blocks.note: the last letter of tapE, placed inside

explanation.surface: Some liquid in a hole beneath the ground being sealed off with tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underground' pulls towards caves and trains; it is the definition in its sense of clandestine.
explanation.definitionFit: Underground activity is secret, hidden from the authorities, as is anything top-secret.

clue.text: 007 perhaps sat upon by his boss a shade (7)

indicators.note: in a down entry, M sits on top of AGENT

blocks.note: M is James Bond's boss in the films

explanation.surface: James Bond being squashed under his boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shade' reads as one unit, but the A is part of the wordplay, closing the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red shade of colour.

clue.text: Antsy energy provider upset, switched over fuels (7)

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset turns SUN upside down
the letters of OVER are switched around
ERVO is fed into NUS, as fuel goes into an engine

explanation.surface: A power company in turmoil after a change of fuel supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all utility business, so 'energy provider' reads as a company; it is the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Antsy is informal for restless and on edge, which is nervous.

clue.text: Came across books about family emblem? (5)

indicators.note: turns the whole string round

blocks.note: OT = Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Stumbling on some books about heraldry.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a totem is a clan's emblem rather than a family crest.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is a natural object or animal adopted as the emblem of a clan or family group.

clue.text: Hat-wearing duke is feature of Don Quixote? (5)

indicators.note: a head wears a hat on the outside, so the hat's letters sit round the duke

blocks.note: tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: A nobleman in a hat, Quixote-style, as a feature of the novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the thin definition: a tilde (~) is a mark over Spanish letters, and Spanish is Don Quixote's language, not his spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The tilde is the wavy accent that marks Spanish text such as Cervantes' novel.

clue.text: Cactus inhabiting moor for the duration (9)

indicators.note: to inhabit is to live within, so the cactus lives inside the moor word

blocks.note: mescal is a small cactus (also called peyote)
to moor a boat is to tie it up

explanation.surface: A cactus growing on open moorland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' reads as heathland, where a cactus would be out of place; it is the verb, tie up.
explanation.definitionFit: A timescale is the period over which something happens: its duration.

clue.text: PM on top of border chaos (6)

indicators.note: in a down entry MAY sits above HEM

blocks.note: Theresa May, a British Prime Minister
a hem is the border of a garment

explanation.surface: A political headline about a Prime Minister handling a border crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: PM tempts you towards the afternoon abbreviation, but here it is a Prime Minister, Theresa May.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name violent, noisy disorder; mayhem was once a legal term for maiming.

clue.text: Temporary work secured by youngster (3-2)

indicators.note: something secured is held fast inside, so the youngster holds the work

blocks.note: a pup is a young animal, or a cheeky youngster

explanation.surface: A teenager landing a casual summer job.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells a teenager's holiday job; 'Temporary' is the definition, as in a pop-up shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A modern sense: a shop or event set up briefly and then gone is described as pop-up.

clue.text: Tree-hugging Russian leader, dear me! (9)

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap your arms round, so the leader's letters wrap round the tree

blocks.note: Gorby, nickname of Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader

explanation.surface: A Russian leader caught hugging a tree, to general surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Gorblimey is a British exclamation of surprise, a corruption of 'God blind me'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise or dismay.

clue.text: Where one might feed an adolescent on chocolate primarily (7)

indicators.note: AN TEEN is placed after C
primarily = in the first place, so only the word's first letter counts

explanation.surface: A parent wondering where to feed a chocolate-mad teenager.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer belongs to the scene: a school canteen is exactly where a teenager is fed.
explanation.definitionFit: A canteen is a place where meals are served, in a school or workplace.

clue.text: Bit of a strain on old English chair (7)

indicators.note: VERSE is set on the middle of OE

blocks.note: a strain is a tune or song; a verse is one part of it

explanation.surface: A strain put on an antique English chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chair' looks like furniture, the antique sort, but it is the verb: to chair a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Chair is the verb: to chair a meeting is to preside over and supervise it.

clue.text: They say I’m quiet six days of the week, however … sweet! (3-5,6)

indicators.note: what they say is heard, not spelt

blocks.clueFragment: I’m quiet six days of the week, however
blocks.note: quiet six days, however on the seventh (Sunday) I scream

explanation.surface: Someone confessing they keep quiet all week, then burst out on the seventh day.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a riddle: quiet six days, but on the remaining day, Sunday, I scream. Said together, 'I scream Sunday' is the dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: 'sweet' is the British word for the dessert course, and this is a dessert of ice cream with toppings.

clue.text: Skin blister’s back in plague (9)

definitions.note: 'Skin' is used attributively, as in 'skin cells', matching the adjective

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter
in = inside, so the letter is placed within the plague word

explanation.surface: A skin blister as a symptom of plague.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is medical throughout, so 'Skin blister' reads as one symptom; the definition is only 'Skin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Epidermic means of the epidermis, the outer layer of skin.

clue.text: Something retired people put on finally opening in nearby city (9)

indicators.note: finally = at the very end, so the word's last letter is taken
in = inside, so the letter is placed within the city word

explanation.surface: Pensioners attending the opening of something in a nearby city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' suggests pensioners; it means gone to bed, which is when a nightgown is put on.
explanation.definitionFit: People who have retired for the night put on nightwear such as a nightgown.

clue.text: Loosen tight nut on corner (8)

indicators.note: tight = drunk, so the letters reel about
in a down entry, UNT sits on ANGLE

explanation.surface: Instructions for easing a tight nut stuck on a corner bracket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' fits a stuck nut, but it means drunk, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: freeing knots or snarls in rope or hair loosens them.

clue.text: Hairpieces got coloured brown in the end — this colour would have been worse (9,5)

definitions.text: this colour would have been worse

indicators.note: coloured = distorted, so the letters rearrange
in the end = at the finish, so the word's last letter is taken

explanation.surface: Wigs dyed an unfortunate brown, though a worse colour was on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole closing remark: the colour that would have been worse than brown for a wig.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistachio green is a pale yellowish-green, a dreadful colour for hair.

clue.text: Good joke — bad joke in it? (7)

blocks.note: British slang for something first-rate, as with 'a real corker'
a Christmas table novelty, pulled apart to reveal a groan-worthy joke

explanation.surface: Weighing up whether a joke is good or bad.
explanation.walkthrough: A Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled apart at British Christmas dinners, containing a paper hat and a terrible joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A cracker is British slang for a first-rate thing, and a cracker joke is proverbially bad.

clue.text: Popular dishes that accompany offal? (7)

explanation.surface: Favourite side dishes to serve with offal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface serves offal with sides, but offal is the definition: the question mark flags that offal is an animal's insides.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the internal organs of an animal, its insides.

clue.text: Formal wear picked up for club entertainer (6)

indicators.note: picked up by the ear, as a radio signal is

blocks.note: a DJ is a dinner jacket; say the letters and spell out the sound

explanation.surface: Dressing up in black tie for a night at a club.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a DJ is a dinner jacket, the tuxedo; saying those letters gives the spelt-out DEEJAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A deejay (disc jockey) plays records to entertain a club crowd.

clue.text: Chosen artist, one of seven sisters (7)

explanation.surface: An artist chosen from a family of seven sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven sisters are the Pleiades of Greek myth (and the star cluster), and Electra is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Electra is one of the Pleiades, the seven daughters of Atlas.

clue.text: No more food for breakfast (5)

blocks.note: slang for finished, done for, as said to someone in deep trouble

explanation.surface: Being told there is nothing left to eat for breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No more food' runs together as one complaint; the split comes after 'No more', slang for done for.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang 'toast' means finished, done for, no more; toast is also a breakfast staple.

clue.text: Recollection of something essential, like one of your five a day? (7)

definitions.text: one of your five a day?

indicators.note: re-collect: gather the letters again, from the back

explanation.surface: Trying to remember something important, possibly a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five a day' is the UK health advice to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables daily; a satsuma is a kind of mandarin orange.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma counts as one of the recommended five daily portions of fruit and veg.

clue.text: Wedding something painful, bachelor a no-show? (5)

indicators.note: the B fails to appear, so it drops out

blocks.note: a bunion is a painful swelling on the foot

explanation.surface: A painful wedding where the groom never turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the bachelor a groom who fails to appear, which suits the deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: marriage joins two people, and union is the formal word for that joining.

clue.text: Awkward situation with verbal agreement — stuffed! (3-6)

indicators.note: spoken, so sound PACT and spell PACKED

explanation.surface: A tricky spot ended by a spoken deal, followed by a cry of dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Verbal agreement' looks like a handshake deal, but 'verbal' is the sound signal on PACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Jam-packed means crammed full, stuffed.

clue.text: Outstanding fellow in green trousers (5)

indicators.note: used as a verb: pockets, so the answer sits inside

explanation.surface: An exceptional man in green trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing; it is the verb, to pocket. 'Outstanding' means unpaid, not excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Outstanding in its money sense, unpaid, which is what owing means of a debt.

clue.text: Boat ending in Germany with crew from there? (5)

indicators.note: an ending is where a word finishes, so its last letter is taken

blocks.note: German for eight, a rowing crew

explanation.surface: A boat finishing in Germany with a local crew aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: A rowing eight is a crew, and 'from there' asks for the German word, ACHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by kind: a yacht is a sailing or motor boat, often for pleasure or racing.

clue.text: On-screen cast interrupted by a sympathetic character (9)

indicators.note: cast = thrown, so the letters land in a new order
A breaks into the rearranged letters

explanation.surface: A film cast featuring a likeable character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' and 'character' both belong to film, so 'sympathetic character' reads as a role; resonance is a sympathetic vibration.
explanation.definitionFit: Resonance is sympathetic vibration, the character of a sound that sets others ringing in sympathy.
